hints: Look at tissue X in Fig. 5.1 - it is pale, solid-looking tissue outside the airway wall. Think what happens to air pressure inside the bronchus during breathing in and out.
walkthrough:
Spot Tissue X**
Tissue X is cartilage. You can tell by the solid plate of tissue with scattered cells in lacunae surrounding the bronchus.

Why Support Matters**
During ventilation the pressure inside the bronchus falls. Without rigid support the soft wall would be sucked closed. Cartilage is strong but flexible, so it holds the airway open and keeps air flowing to the alveoli.
Final answer: Holds the bronchus / airway open and prevents it from collapsing when air pressure falls.

hints: Compare Fig. 5.1 with what you remember of a trachea cross-section - in the bronchus the cartilage looks like broken, irregular chunks.
Recall the classic shape of tracheal cartilage and how evenly it is spaced to keep the long trachea permanently open but flexible for swallowing.
walkthrough:
Bronchus Pattern In Fig. 5.1**
In the bronchus, cartilage is present as irregular plates or chunks, not as neat rings. This is because the airway is branching.

Trachea Pattern**
In the trachea, cartilage is arranged as regular C-shaped incomplete rings stacked along the length. The gap in the C allows the oesophagus to expand during swallowing, while the regular spacing gives continuous support.
Final answer: In the trachea cartilage forms incomplete / C-shaped rings; the rings are more regularly distributed along the length of the trachea.

hints: Tissue Y lines the inside of the bronchus. Think of the two cell types you find there - one with tiny hair-like structures, one that makes a sticky secretion.
Link each cell type to its job in cleaning air - what traps dust and bacteria, and what moves that sticky layer upward?
walkthrough:
Two Cell Team**
Tissue Y is ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. Do not mix them up - cilia belong to the ciliated cells, mucus comes from goblet cells.

Trapping Then Clearing**
Goblet cells secrete sticky mucus that traps dust, bacteria and other pathogens from inhaled air. The cilia on the ciliated cells then beat in a coordinated wave to sweep the mucus up toward the throat to be swallowed. Together this is the mucociliary escalator that protects the alveoli.
Final answer: Ciliated epithelial cells have cilia to sweep / waft mucus up and away; goblet cells secrete mucus to trap dust / bacteria / pathogens.

hints: Think how volume grows much faster than surface area as an animal gets bigger - which elephant will have more volume for each unit of skin surface?
walkthrough:
Size And Ratio Rule**
As size increases, volume increases by the cube while surface area increases only by the square. So the bigger adult has a much larger volume relative to its surface, giving a smaller surface area to volume ratio.
Final answer: The adult / larger elephant has a smaller surface area to volume ratio than the baby elephant.

hints: Start from body plan - an elephant has millions of cells deep inside the body, not just a surface layer.
Think about activity and respiration - every cell needs oxygen for aerobic respiration and needs carbon dioxide removed quickly.
Recall why diffusion alone fails for large animals - think about speed over distance and surface area to volume ratio from part (i).
walkthrough:
Many Cells Deep Inside**
Elephants are large and multicellular. Most cells are buried deep inside, far from the outside air.

High Demand**
All those cells respire aerobically, so they need a large, continuous supply of oxygen and rapid removal of carbon dioxide, especially in active tissues like muscle.

Diffusion Cannot Cope**
Diffusion over long distances is very slow, and the small surface area to volume ratio means the body surface cannot supply enough gas by diffusion alone. A specialised gas exchange system with a large surface and ventilation plus a transport system is needed.

Final answer: Multicellular with many cells; high demand for oxygen to supply all cells and remove carbon dioxide; diffusion across body surface is too slow and diffusion distance to inner cells is too long to meet needs.

hints: Start by counting chains - collagen is not a single polypeptide or a globular protein.
Picture how those chains are wound together and what holds them in that shape.
Think why the chains can pack so tightly - a very small amino acid appears at regular intervals.
Recall where that small amino acid sits in the helix to allow close packing.
walkthrough:
Three Chains**
A collagen molecule consists of three separate polypeptide chains, not one.

Triple Helix**
The three chains coil around each other to form a triple helix. They lie very close together as a tight, rope-like coil.

Held By Hydrogen Bonds**
Hydrogen bonds form between the chains and hold the three strands together, giving great stability.

Glycine Repeat**
Every third amino acid in each chain is glycine. Glycine is the smallest amino acid and faces the inside of the helix, so the three chains can pack tightly together without bulky side chains getting in the way.

Final answer: Made of three polypeptide chains wound into a triple helix held together by hydrogen bonds in a tight coil; every third amino acid is glycine, with glycine on the inside of the helix allowing close packing.

hints: Think about how many collagen molecules are arranged together in a fibre, rather than the three chains within one molecule.
Consider how links between neighbouring molecules or the positions of their ends can prevent weak points.
walkthrough:
Use the fibre level of organisation**
Many collagen molecules lie parallel within fibrils, which form fibres.

Give one accepted strengthening feature**
Strong covalent cross-links between molecules help hold the structure together. Staggered molecular ends also prevent a continuous weak line across the fibre. One appropriate feature is sufficient for this one-mark response; parallel arrangement is also accepted by the official scheme.
Final answer: Strong covalent cross-links between collagen molecules strengthen the fibre.
